item.title: Drew Breunig bakes a functional NES emulator into Qwen3.5-4B model weights
item.description:
Drew Breunig bakes a functional NES emulator into Qwen3.5-4B model weights

On October 30, 2026, developer Drew Breunig released “nesformer,” a project that integrates a working Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) 6502 CPU emulator directly into the weights of the Qwen3.5-4B model.

🔍 Overview

Inspired by Divyansh Agrawal’s “qwenputer,” this project allows users to run NES ROMs inside the Qwen model. While the system is functional and capable of running games like Super Mario Bros, it currently operates very slowly. Breunig noted the project was built “just for fun.”

🧩 How it works

To build the system, Breunig used Opus 5.5 with specific prompts to analyze the original “qwenputer” article and explore the feasibility of emulating NES chips and RAM using language model weights.

  • Emulation Target: The system emulates the 6502 CPU and RAM of the Nintendo Entertainment System.
  • Validation: During development, Opus 5.5 utilized a collection of NES CPU conformance tests released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow to ensure accuracy.
  • Methodology: The system was designed to explore whether smaller, faster models could eventually reach standard clockspeeds for hardware emulation.

⚙️ Key details

Attribute Specification
Base Model Qwen3.5-4B
Processor Emulated NES 6502 CPU
Tested ROMs Super Mario Bros
Logic Foundation Weights-based emulation

🚀 Availability

The project is available with the necessary model weights and a command-line interface (CLI). Users can run the system by pointing the CLI at a compatible NES ROM file.

#Qwen #Emulation #RetroGaming #LLM

Source: dbreunig/nesformer

item.title: Spawn Game Uses Autonomous AI Agents to Ship Code Hourly
item.description:
Spawn Game Uses Autonomous AI Agents to Ship Code Hourly

Spawn, a massively multiplayer gaming environment, is being built and updated by a swarm of AI agents that modify live code and ship changes every hour.

🔍 Overview

  • Players interact with an in‑game agent called Savi by sending prompts that modify the game world.
  • A user report describes creating a castle, summoning a dragon, and riding the dragon around the castle on a phone.

🤖 Autonomous Development

  • Development is driven by a swarm of Fable‑powered agents that cost over $3 million in tokens per month (“we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens”).
  • The agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly.
  • 60 % of work originates from a production error, a Savi bug report, an odd log entry, or a feature request.
  • Savi files bugs herself; when a bug is hit, it is routed to an agent that decides whether it is a real bug, something not to fix, or an intentional design decision.
  • Usually the resulting change is delivered to the user within an hour, accompanied by a message in the same chat.
  • An hour without a ship is treated as a SEV‑0 incident, the most severe kind of incident.
  • Agents can retain only a few hours of work in their “head”; shipping faster helps them stay coherent.
  • A broken change can be rolled back in 30 seconds, exactly where it broke and nowhere else.
  • When a monitor or log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and the team sometimes breaks things on purpose to verify recovery paths.

📊 Model Variants

Model Outcome
Fable 5 / 5.1 Enabled the current level of autonomy (as cited by Jacob).
Opus 5.5 Not sufficient for their needs (“doesn’t quite hack it for them”).
GPT‑6 Astra Applied security fixes by turning off every feature, leaving the product non‑functional.

⚙️ Incident Handling Loop

  • An alert triggers or awakens an agent responsible for the incident.
  • The agent evaluates the bug, classifies it, and either ships a fix or decides on another action.
  • The rapid ship‑and‑rollback capability keeps the production environment tight and responsive.

💡 Why It Matters

  • The system creates a continuous, hour‑long feedback loop that only works because shipping never stops.
  • It demonstrates that a game can serve as a substrate for testing the limits of today’s coding agents.
  • The author notes uncertainty about applying this style to higher‑stakes software, but observes that it is surprisingly effective for a game.
  • Extreme experiments, such as the GPT‑6 Astra security overhaul, highlight both the potential and the risks of autonomous code modification.

#AIAgents #GameDevelopment #AutonomousCoding #SoftwareEngineering

Source: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models

item.title: AI Integration Enables Drawing and Editing draw.io Diagrams via Chat
item.description:
AI Integration Enables Drawing and Editing draw.io Diagrams via Chat

Users can now draw and edit draw.io diagrams by chatting with an AI across web, desktop, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server environments.

🔍 Overview

By describing a diagram in a single sentence, the AI generates it directly on a real draw.io canvas. Users can subsequently edit the canvas by hand or select specific shapes and instruct the AI on what changes to make.

⚙️ Key Features

  • Diagram Generation: Create architecture diagrams, flowcharts, sequence diagrams, and other visuals from a single sentence. Built-in icon libraries include AWS, Azure, GCP, and Kubernetes.
  • File & Image Inputs: Upload screenshots or hand sketches for the AI to redraw. Upload PDF, Markdown, code, or other text files to generate diagrams based on their contents.
  • Real-Time Streaming & Highlighting: When editing via chat, changes stream directly onto the canvas, and newly modified shapes are highlighted.
  • Targeted Selection Editing: Select specific shapes on the canvas and instruct the AI to modify only the chosen elements.
  • Version Control & Undo: Every AI edit creates a version card featuring a thumbnail. Users can compare versions with the current canvas, restore previous states, or undo changes. Pressing Ctrl+Z on the canvas also reverses an AI edit in a single step.
  • Standard Canvas Controls: Diagrams function as standard draw.io files, supporting manual dragging, restyling, double-clicking to rename, multi-page structures, and animated connectors carrying flowing animations.
  • Export Formats: Files export at any time as .drawio, .png, .svg, or .drawio.svg.

🧩 Supported Diagram Examples

Prompts tested with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code via the MCP server demonstrate a range of diagram generation capabilities:

  • AWS Architecture: Generates a highly available web app across two Availability Zones using AWS icons (Route 53, CloudFront with AWS WAF, Application Load Balancer, ECS Fargate services in private subnets, Aurora PostgreSQL with writer/reader, ElastiCache for Redis, S3, NAT gateways, and CloudWatch).
  • Kubernetes Deployment: Generates a web shop deployment diagram containing an ingress, web and API deployments with services and pods, a Redis StatefulSet with a persistent volume, a ConfigMap, a Secret, and an API autoscaler.
  • Entity-Relationship (ER) Diagrams: Renders ER diagrams for an online shop detailing entities (customers, addresses, orders, order items, products, categories, payments), primary and foreign keys, and relationship cardinalities.
  • BPMN Process Workflows: Renders process flows, such as an expense claim process tracking employee submission, manager approval/rejection, finance receipt checks and payment, and return steps for missing receipts.
  • Customer Journey Maps: Maps customer journeys across five stages (discover, sign up, first payment, everyday use, get help) with actions, touchpoints, feelings, pain points, and opportunities.
  • Animated Connectors: Produces diagrams featuring flowing connector animations, such as transformer architecture diagrams.

🚀 Availability & Specifications

  • Platforms: Accessible as a web app, a desktop application for Windows, macOS, and Linux, and as an MCP server for AI agents including Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and VS Code.
  • Model Provider Support: Supports 25 model providers alongside an OpenAI-compatible preset for custom URLs. User API keys entered in the browser remain locally on the machine. Models that reason display their thinking process.
  • Interface & Languages: Includes dark mode support and offers an interface available in English, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and Japanese.

#drawio #Diagramming #MCPServer #ClaudeCode #AITools

Source: DayuanJiang/next-ai-draw-io

item.title: OpenAI Shows Improved AI‑Based Migration of COBOL and Other Legacy Code
item.description:
OpenAI Shows Improved AI‑Based Migration of COBOL and Other Legacy Code

On October 19, OpenAI announced substantial improvements in its latest AI models’ ability to migrate aging software written in older programming languages into modern code, claiming that the advances could help organizations modernize legacy systems.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenAI highlighted COBOL, a language created in 1959 (“common business‑oriented language”), as a primary target for migration.
  • COBOL underpins critical infrastructure: more than 40 % of online banking, 80 % of in‑person credit‑card transactions, 95 % of ATM transactions, and many government systems such as Social Security, the IRS, and most state services.
  • An estimate puts the annual cost of COBOL’s inefficiencies to the U.S. GDP at around $105 billion.
  • Other legacy languages like Fortran remain in use for scientific computing, weather forecasting, and nuclear‑security code.

🛠️ How it works

  • OpenAI’s blog reported successful migrations of COBOL code to modern languages including C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, and Rust without changing what the original software does.
  • The company emphasizes that a migration is considered successful only if all tests pass.
  • In its own tests, the model‑variant GPT‑6.1 Sol achieved 87 % behavior‑preservation accuracy at low reasoning effort, climbing to 98 % at higher reasoning effort.
  • OpenAI notes that “the evaluations shown… demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.”

📊 Evaluation results

Model Low‑reasoning behavior preservation High‑reasoning behavior preservation
GPT‑6.1 Sol 87 % 98 %
GPT‑6 Astra ~86 % –
GPT‑6 Sol 21 % –
GPT‑5.6 Sol 5 % –

💡 Why it matters

  • Migrating legacy code can reduce the massive economic drag attributed to outdated systems.
  • Modern languages enable easier maintenance, security updates, and integration with current tooling.
  • OpenAI also reported improvements in building database software in various languages, including COBOL.

🗣️ Industry reaction

  • OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines told The Verge that legacy code “is still far from a solved problem” and that the company is listening to developer feedback and exploring better tests.
  • Vadim Zaytsev, associate professor of software evolution at the University of Twente, cautioned that “rewriting code is not the same as replacing a system” and that AI currently plays a limited role in replacing or migrating large COBOL systems.
  • Arie van Deursen of Delft University of Technology described OpenAI’s blog as “superficial,” noting the lack of detail about the migration task and that the benchmark used a relatively simple, well‑defined task.
  • Shares in IBM, which earns revenue helping companies maintain legacy systems, nosedived after Anthropic’s announcement of its own code‑modernization playbook.
  • Anthropic’s Claude Code was promoted as a way to migrate COBOL to Java or Python, but the company provided no performance benchmarks and stated only that “the economics of COBOL modernization have shifted.”

#OpenAI #LegacyCode #CodeMigration #AIModels

Source: Can AI help solve the COBOL code crisis?

item.title: AI tools accelerate retro game decompilation and porting, sparking community turmoil
item.description:
AI tools accelerate retro game decompilation and porting, sparking community turmoil

Retro video games are popping up everywhere lately – often in places they weren’t designed for. Examples include Halo running in a web browser, Wind Waker on the iPhone, and Super Smash Bros. in mixed reality.

🤖 AI’s Role in Decomp & Porting

  • New AI coding tools let hobbyists break games down to their building blocks and rebuild them for hardware they were never meant for.
  • Decomps and recomps (short for decomposition and recomposition) are forms of reverse engineering that traditionally took years; AI has cut those timelines dramatically.
  • AI enables “much faster” work when the developer knows what they want, leading to a surge of new ports on Reddit, X, and GitHub.

📈 Recent Surge & Examples

Game New Platform
Halo Web browser
The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker iPhone
Super Smash Bros. Mixed reality
Command & Conquer: Generals Zero Hour (open‑source) iPhone & iPad
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (using community decomp) Mobile
  • Chris Sotraidis, an AI consultant who works on game ports as a hobby, saw the Generals Zero Hour port and then started a handful of similar ports, including a mobile Ocarina of Time.
  • Within a few weeks he was juggling a dozen projects, noting that this level of productivity “wouldn’t happen without the use of AI.”

⚠️ Preservation Concerns

  • Traditional decomp projects let users pull a game apart to understand how it works; AI‑generated ports can skip that learning step.
  • The ability to quickly “finish” a decomp with AI means the underlying programming decisions may be lost, making faithful restoration harder.
  • More than 90 % of classic games are considered “critically endangered,” so the speed‑first approach risks long‑term drawbacks.

🛠️ Community Impact & Shutdown

  • A community‑focused website that tracked decomp projects shut down, citing AI’s impact.
  • The site’s owner (pseudonym Encounter) wrote:

    “It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way.”

  • The same statement added that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken, with “bad actors” abusing AI to fork projects without meaningful contribution, tearing apart the community fabric.

🌐 Why It Matters

  • AI has turned niche terms like decomp and recomp into headline material and opened experimentation to non‑programmers.
  • At the same time, the rapid, low‑detail nature of many AI‑driven ports clashes with preservationists’ goals of both keeping games playable and understanding their original construction.
  • Epic Games’ shift to “AI‑accelerated development” for an upcoming Disney collaboration illustrates how major studios are also embracing AI, reinforcing its growing influence across the industry.

#AI #GamePreservation #RetroGaming #Decompilation

Source: Retro gaming is being overrun with AI

item.title: Audit Reveals Specification-Oracle Gap in Coding-Agent Benchmarks
item.description:
Audit Reveals Specification-Oracle Gap in Coding-Agent Benchmarks

Coding‑agent benchmarks often phrase a task in natural language while grading it with upstream tests that may require hidden implementation details.

🔍 Overview

  • Benchmarks describe the request in plain text but validate output using tests taken from the original project.
  • Passing those tests can need information the description never provides, such as a constant’s name, a module path, or an exact error message.

🧩 Specification‑Oracle Gap

  • This mismatch is called a specification‑oracle gap.
  • Where the gap exists, a benchmark unintentionally measures an agent’s ability to reproduce upstream implementation details rather than just solving the described problem.

⚙️ How the Gap Was Audited

  • The authors formalised the gap and the inconsistencies introduced by chains of dependent tasks.
  • They built a static audit covering five programming languages that classifies every name‑, path‑, and literal‑level dependency of every scored test.
  • The audit achieved held‑out precision of 89.2 % and recall of 92.9 %.

📊 Findings

  • SWE‑Milestone (98 graded milestones, 35 published runs):
    • 25 milestones contain a test depending on an unstated, non‑inferable name or path.
    • Build units with such a hidden dependency fail in 80.6 % of runs, versus 48.4 % for comparable units without one.
    • Removing a single hidden name from the reference prevents compilation in 126 of 128 cases.
  • The leaderboard ranking remains robust after removing the affected tests, but scores shift within repositories and tend to favour agents that replicate upstream names.
  • Across four additional benchmarks:
    • A third or more of tasks are affected when specifications come from release notes or LLM summaries.
    • Almost none are affected when tasks are screened or written expressly for their tests.
    • The cost of the gap varies with how the harness grades the solutions.

🚀 Release

  • The authors have released the static audit, corrected filter lists, and specification addenda for the community to use.

#AIagents #Benchmarking #SoftwareEngineering #Evaluation

Source: What the Specification Did Not Say: Specification-Oracle Gaps in Test-Graded Coding-Agent Benchmarks

item.title: AI-Enabled Exploits of Longstanding PHP Vulnerabilities Impact Global Websites
item.description:
AI-Enabled Exploits of Longstanding PHP Vulnerabilities Impact Global Websites

Two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language have placed a significant portion of the internet at risk, leading to widespread site shutdowns and millions of attack attempts.

🔍 Overview

PHP underpins up to 70 percent of websites, including WordPress, Drupal, Wikipedia, DeviantArt, and 4Chan. Security firm Wiz has described these vulnerabilities as “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered … in software history.”

🧩 How it works

The vulnerabilities have existed in PHP for roughly 20 years. While previously exploiting them “required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” powerful AI models have now made it easier to turn these obscure bugs into dangerous vulnerabilities.

⚙️ Key details

  • Scope: Affects every version of PHP dating back approximately 20 years.
  • Attack Volume: Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reported thousands of exploit attempts in the 10 hours before public disclosure, jumping to “hundreds of thousands” in the following 2 hours, and reaching “millions” by the following night.
  • Official Guidance: The UK’s National Cyber Security Center and the NSA Cybersecurity account on X recommended that organizations take systems offline if “an immediate update is not feasible.”

💡 Why it matters

Because many versions of PHP are no longer supported, some sites cannot be patched. This has led to the following impacts:

Entity Impact
Internet Archive Briefly forced offline; later patched and secured
World Quest Permanently shutting down due to older tech
Save My Demonic World Permanently shutting down due to older tech
Pokémon Home & Pokémon Champions Taken offline
4Chan & DeviantArt Temporarily shut down
Dutch & Finnish Government Agencies Some sites taken down as a precaution

#PHP #Cybersecurity #AI #WebDevelopment

Source: PHP: The three little letters wreaking havoc across the web

item.title: Rescale Deploys AI-Driven Triage Agent to Automate Test Failure Classification
item.description:
Rescale Deploys AI-Driven Triage Agent to Automate Test Failure Classification

Rescale, the digital engineering platform built for the AI era, has released an AI‑driven triage agent that automatically classifies and routes nightly end‑to‑end test failures.

🔍 Overview

  • The agent is part of Rescale’s AI‑Driven Development Lifecycle (AI‑DLC) framework and runs on AWS.
  • It integrates with Rescale’s existing Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS).

🛠️ Problem

  • Every engineering team knows the ritual of a nightly test suite that fails.
  • An on‑call engineer pulls logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning.
  • At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full‑time job hidden inside an on‑call rotation.
  • Hundreds of test cases run in the suite; each failure requires classification, prioritization, and routing to the appropriate team.
  • After routing, engineers must gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems and several source repositories before debugging can begin.
  • Unresolved failures can block weekly production releases and pull several teams into hours of coordination.

🤖 Solution – AI‑Driven Development Lifecycle (AI‑DLC)

  • AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing.
  • Humans validate and steer at each step; AI executes, humans decide.
  • Development is organized into focused group sessions:
    • Mob Elaboration – defining requirements together.
    • Mob Construction – building together while AI handles implementation.
  • In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answer the AI’s questions collectively and approve each plan before the AI proceeds, eliminating assumptions.

⚙️ Implementation

  • The triage agent automates classification and routing of nightly end‑to‑end test failures.
  • It runs as a step within Rescale’s Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline on Amazon EKS.
  • When a nightly Playwright suite of hundreds of test cases produces failures, the pipeline triggers the triage agent pod.
  • The team moved from problem definition to a staging deployment in five days and to production within weeks.

🚀 Impact

  • Engineers no longer spend significant time on the repetitive but critical task of manually classifying test failures.
  • Automation frees engineers to focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems.
  • The solution demonstrates how AI can be applied across the engineering lifecycle—from planning and design through testing and operations—while keeping engineers accountable for the result.

#AI #DevOps #Automation #AWS

Source: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Eon Optimizes Multi-Cloud AI Agent Operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.description:
Eon Optimizes Multi-Cloud AI Agent Operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

Eon, a company that manages production incidents across AWS, Azure, and GCP, has successfully streamlined its AI agent infrastructure by implementing Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This transition replaced complex, localized processes with a centralized, managed gateway that enables secure, unified access to operational tooling for both human engineers and autonomous agents.

🔍 Overview

Managing AI-powered products across multiple clouds created significant overhead for Eon. As their toolset expanded, the team faced challenges with credential management, disparate network boundaries, and inconsistent access policies. Previously, new engineers spent two days configuring credentials and local Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to begin investigating incidents. By deploying Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, this onboarding time has been reduced to approximately two minutes.

🧩 How it works

Eon transitioned from local, fragmented MCP processes to a centralized architecture using the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stack. The system functions as follows:

  • Centralized Gateway: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway serves as a single front door, converting local MCP servers into remote HTTP endpoints.
  • Identity and Auth: Corporate SSO is federated through Amazon Cognito, while agents authenticate using client_credentials grants. Amazon API Gateway manages the OAuth entry point.
  • Authorization: Cedar policies enforce strict controls on which principals can invoke specific tools.
  • Security: Production tools are set to read-only mode, with write operations restricted to low-impact tasks such as commenting on PRs or tickets.

⚙️ Key details

Capability Description
AgentCore Gateway Managed gateway with identity federation and policy enforcement.
AgentCore Runtime Hosts logic to convert local MCP servers to remote HTTP endpoints.
AgentCore Identity Manages authentication protocols for humans and agents.
Resource Management Discovers and classifies cloud resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP.

💡 Why it matters

  • Reduced Operational Complexity: Eliminated the need for per-tool credential management and manual rotation.
  • Improved Efficiency: Removed the need for VPC peering or PrivateLink per account, reducing networking overhead and setup time.
  • Cost Optimization: Continuous deduplicated backup of cloud resources has reduced storage costs by up to 50 percent according to Eon’s internal measurements.
  • Unified Access: Provided a consistent interface for engineers and autonomous SRE agents to access logs, metrics, and deployment information across multiple clouds in a single session.

#AmazonBedrock #AIAgents #CloudOps #MultiCloud #Engineering

Source: How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Impact of Coding Agents on the Programming Profession
item.description:
Impact of Coding Agents on the Programming Profession

The emergence of coding agents is altering the nature of professional programming, specifically regarding the role of solving logic puzzles in software development.

💡 Why it matters

The shift toward LLMs impacts programmers differently based on their professional motivations:

  • For programmers who thrive on building working systems and do not care deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are described as “the gift that keeps on giving.”
  • For programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code, the loss is described as “very real.”

Historically, programming was characterized by the following:

  • Professionals were paid to work on “tricky little logic puzzles,” with higher pay for trickier puzzles.
  • Programmers set the strategy, defined the timeline, and determined what was and was not possible.
  • Regular people were unable to perform these tasks, making even simple puzzles valuable.

#LLMs #CodingAgents #Programming #SoftwareDevelopment

Source: My obituary for programming

item.title: Lean Rada Describes Inline Rendering Trick Using document.currentScript
item.description:
Lean Rada Describes Inline Rendering Trick Using document.currentScript

On 17th October 2026, Lean Rada described a trick for inline rendering that utilizes the document.currentScript property. This method allows a tiny inline <script> element to replace itself with dynamic content when a page loads.

🧩 How it works

The trick functions by having a script reference its own position in the document to swap itself for new data.

  • Basic Implementation: An inline script can use document.currentScript.replaceWith(new Date().getFullYear()) to replace the tag with the current year.
  • Shortcut Function: A shortcut can be defined as $=(...n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(...n) to simplify the process.
  • Template Language: This shortcut creates a tiny template language, allowing for inline syntax such as <script>$(new Date().getFullYear())</script>.

⚙️ Key details

Item Description
Core Property document.currentScript
Replacement Method .replaceWith()
Shortcut Definition $=(…n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(…n)
Creator Lean Rada

item.title: Microsoft Research unveils Magnetar: Faster, language‑agnostic zero‑knowledge proofs
item.description:
Microsoft Research unveils Magnetar: Faster, language‑agnostic zero‑knowledge proofs

Magnetar is the newest zero‑knowledge proof system from Microsoft Research. It can prove the correct execution of programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster than earlier comparable systems, and its security relies only on standard hash functions.

🔍 Overview

  • Runs a workload and produces, together with the output, a short cryptographic proof that the program ran correctly.
  • The proof is small and can be checked in milliseconds by anyone, without rerunning the program, without trusting the prover, and without needing the input data.
  • Verification can be passed on to others who need the same assurance.

🧩 How it works

  • Zero‑knowledge proofs allow a prover to convince a verifier that a computation was performed correctly while revealing nothing about private inputs.
  • Magnetar’s processor description builds on the Phalanx idea of exploiting repetition in a processor’s instruction cycle to accelerate proof generation.
  • The system is instantiated with hash‑based cryptographic primitives, eliminating the need for a trusted setup and avoiding elliptic‑curve‑based constructions.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supported languages: Rust, Go, C.
  • Performance: 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems.
  • Proof size and verification: Proofs are short; verification takes milliseconds.
  • Security basis: Relies only on standard hash functions, not on elliptic curves.
  • Zero‑knowledge property: The proof reveals no information about inputs that should stay private.

📚 Background

  • Zero‑knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s; the concept of proving program execution has been around nearly as long.
  • Early practical approaches were limited to small programs and required either a layered sum‑check protocol or elliptic‑curve cryptography with a trusted setup.
  • In 2019, the Spartan system returned to the sum‑check approach, supporting general‑purpose programs without a trusted setup and allowing different cryptographic building blocks.
  • Phalanx (2021) demonstrated how to use repeated processor steps to achieve an order‑of‑magnitude speed improvement over Spartan.
  • Magnetar is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero‑knowledge proofs practical.

🔐 Security & Quantum Considerations

  • Many prior proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by sufficiently powerful quantum computers.
  • Microsoft’s Quantum Safe Program aims to move products and services to post‑quantum cryptography by 2029.
  • Post‑quantum proof systems exist but often rely on newer cryptographic functions that have not undergone decades of scrutiny.
  • Magnetar’s reliance on standard hash functions avoids the unproven assumptions of newer primitives.

#ZeroKnowledge #Cryptography #MicrosoftResearch #VerifiableComputing

Source: Magnetar brings faster, simpler, quantum-ready zero-knowledge proofs

item.title: Microsoft Launches Xbox Labs to Explore AI‑Driven Game Modding
item.description:
Microsoft Launches Xbox Labs to Explore AI‑Driven Game Modding

Microsoft announced a new Xbox Labs group to experiment with AI‑powered decompilation and recompilation of games, turning emerging ideas into experiences for players and developers.

🔍 Overview

  • Xbox Labs is described as “a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.” – Xbox CEO Asha Sharma
  • The group will focus on rapid emergence of mods that use AI models to remix games in ways rarely seen before.
  • Microsoft has already seen mods such as skateboarding added to Call of Duty and Halo running in a web browser.

🤖 AI in Game Modding

  • AI models are helping modders decompile, recompile, and merge code from different titles.
  • Sharma notes that “coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software,” and that games share many of those same properties.
  • Players spend more than 72 billion hours a year on Xbox games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.
  • Microsoft plans to share any tools and learnings from Xbox Labs with the broader developer community.

⚙️ Experiments & Findings

  • Recent weeks have seen classic PC builds translated to run on Apple Silicon and ported to browsers via WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90 % global browser support.
  • Modders are achieving results similar to Microsoft’s Xbox backward‑compatibility program—running old games on modern hardware—without the business‑model restrictions Microsoft traditionally faces.

item.title: Industry Skips to Agentic AI Architecture, Bypassing Intermediate Steps
item.description:
Industry Skips to Agentic AI Architecture, Bypassing Intermediate Steps

The AI ecosystem is increasingly adopting the fourth architecture – agentic AI – even though it jumps over the three earlier, lower‑cost rungs.

🔎 Overview

  • Four ways to build on a language model are commonly presented as a taxonomy: LLM, RAG, AI agent, and agentic AI.
  • The single variable that separates them is who decides how many model calls happen.
  • The industry is “skipping to the fourth,” moving straight to an orchestrated, multi‑model setup.

🪜 The Four Architecture Rungs

Rung Name Who controls the model calls? Added component(s)
1 LLM Your code (single prompt) –
2 RAG Your code (retriever + LLM) Retriever that pulls indexed chunks
3 AI agent The model (handed control flow) –
4 Agentic AI Orchestrator drives one or more models Orchestrator + shared state

⚙️ Rung Details

  • Rung 1 – LLM
    • Takes a prompt and generates a token‑by‑token response.
    • No lookup, memory, or verification.
    • A single well‑constructed call is the highest‑reliability, lowest‑latency, cheapest option.
    • Works best when everything the model needs is already in front of it.
  • Rung 2 – Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG)
    • Query first goes to a retriever, which searches an indexed knowledge base and returns relevant chunks.
    • The LLM receives the original query plus the retrieved chunks and generates a grounded response.
    • “Grounded is not the same as correct.”
    • Retrieval changes what the model sees, not what it does with that input.
    • Almost every RAG failure is a retrieval failure, not a generation failure; there are six distinct failure points, only one lives in the model.
  • Rung 3 – AI Agent
    • Hands control flow to the model itself.
    • The model decides how many calls to make during execution.
  • Rung 4 – Agentic AI
    • Adds an orchestrator that drives one or more models toward a shared objective over shared state.
    • The orchestrator and shared state are the new additions, not the number of agents.

💰 Cost & Performance Implications

  • Moving from RAG to an agentic AI setup measured 36× the cost.
  • Rungs 3 and 4 exhibit full distributions of latency and cost; the tail (not the median) determines the bill and the p95 latency.
  • The single handoff – the moment control flow moves from your code into the model – is the most consequential architectural decision and is often made by accident.

🛠️ Common Failure Modes

  • The first three rungs share the same fundamental failure: the model cannot distinguish what it knows from what it generates.
  • In RAG, the dominant failure mode is retrieval – the retriever may return irrelevant or missing chunks.
  • Climbing a rung to fix a poor output often adds a new problem layer; a bad rung‑1 result is more often a prompt issue than an architecture issue.

📈 Why the Handoff Matters

  • Deciding who controls the number of model calls determines cost, latency, and reliability.
  • Accidental handoff to the model (rung 3 or 4) can expose hidden tail costs and latency spikes.
  • Understanding the ladder of control helps teams choose the appropriate rung for their workload rather than defaulting to the most complex option.

item.title: Encore expands platform for building production systems with real infrastructure
item.description:
Encore expands platform for building production systems with real infrastructure

Encore released an update that adds new capabilities for building, testing, and deploying production‑grade systems using real infrastructure throughout the development lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

Encore is the infrastructure platform for the intelligence era, where engineers and AI agents build production systems without waiting on infrastructure.

🧩 How It Works

  • Run and validate with real infrastructure locally and in preview environments, then deploy to your own AWS or GCP account.
  • Declare the resources your app needs (databases, Pub/Sub, object storage, caches, cron jobs, secrets) directly in your code, and encore run starts the whole system locally with real Postgres, real Pub/Sub semantics, and distributed tracing.
  • Each declaration becomes a node in Encore’s application graph.
  • Encore runs the migrations and stands up local equivalents on encore run, and provisions the cloud equivalents on deploy.
  • When you push a change that adds or modifies a resource, Encore diffs the application graph against the environment, provisions whatever is missing in your AWS or GCP account, and rolls out the new code against it.
  • Encore separates application semantics from environment-specific configuration.
  • In code, you define what resources your app needs, not how each environment should configure them.
  • That keeps services portable across clouds, regions, accounts, scale profiles, and local development.
  • Encore provisions every resource with sane production defaults, then helps you manage configuration separately from your application code.

⚙️ Key Features

  • Encore platform dashboard: easy to use knobs for all common settings like process allocation, instance sizes, replicas, etc.
  • Your AWS or GCP console: tweak anything directly in your cloud provider console.
  • Encore picks up the changes on the next deploy.
  • IaC: manage config for Encore‑provisioned resources alongside the rest of your infrastructure via the Terraform provider.
  • The same infrastructure model runs locally, in per‑PR preview environments, and in production.
  • Local: encore run starts the whole system locally: real Postgres, real Pub/Sub semantics, type‑safe service‑to‑service calls, plus a local dashboard with distributed tracing.
  • Infrastructure namespaces let multiple branches or agents work in parallel with isolated state.
  • Open a pull request and Encore sets up an ephemeral environment and (optionally) branches databases from a seed environment.
  • This Lets you do end‑to‑end validation against before merging to a shared staging environment.
  • Production: Push to deploy.
  • Encore diffs the application graph against the environment, provisions what is missing in your AWS or GCP account, wires up least‑privilege IAM based on the application’s code paths, and rolls out the new code.

🚀 Availability

The update is available to users who already have Encore set up on AWS or GCP and can be accessed through the standard encore run and deployment commands.

💡 Why It Matters

By letting developers define what resources are needed rather than how each environment configures them, Encore makes services portable across clouds, regions, and accounts while keeping configuration separate from application code. This reduces waiting time for infrastructure, enables safe end‑to‑end validation in preview environments, and enforces least‑privilege permissions automatically.

item.title: AI Teams Drop Chat UIs for Headless API‑Driven Agent Architecture
item.description:
AI Teams Drop Chat UIs for Headless API‑Driven Agent Architecture

Over forty early‑stage software companies have quietly deprecated their primary web chat interfaces in the last quarter, replacing them with raw REST endpoints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and direct SDK hooks.

🔍 Overview

  • Over forty early‑stage software companies have quietly deprecated their primary web chat interfaces in the last quarter.
  • Instead of pushing users into conversational loops, these teams are shipping raw REST endpoints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and direct SDK hooks.
  • Companies that previously marketed themselves as enterprise AI copilots are ripping out their frontends entirely.
  • They are pivoting toward background microservices, event‑driven agent frameworks, and direct API integrations that run headlessly inside customer infrastructure.

🛠️ How it works

  • Standard web chat applications carry massive prompt context wrappers, system instructions, and historical conversation arrays that bloat API payload sizes.
  • Passing thousands of conversation tokens back and forth for a simple state change costs real money and adds hundreds of milliseconds of unnecessary network latency.
  • Raw APIs with strict JSON mode enforce structured parameters directly at the inference layer.
  • Systems expose their capabilities via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or Agent Communication Protocol (ACP).
  • Instead of holding an open HTTP streaming connection while a user waits for a chat window to finish typing, requests enter background task queues like Redis or Kafka.
  • Background agents powered by OpenClaw or Hermes Agent pick up the payload, execute the sequence headlessly, and trigger webhooks upon completion.
  • Memory frameworks like Mem0 and Zep handle contextual state outside the model’s context window, while state persists in structured vector databases like Qdrant or Pinecone rather than accumulating in a long chat history string.

⚙️ Key details

  • Startups were spending 40% of their engineering hours troubleshooting Server‑Sent Events (SSE) streaming bugs, markdown formatting errors, and frontend state sync issues instead of refining model execution logic.
  • When OpenAI rolled out GPT‑5.6 Sol Ultra and Anthropic introduced Claude Sonnet 5, the raw reasoning capability reached a point where manual prompt back‑and‑forth became a bottleneck rather than a feature.
  • Freeform chat output produces unpredictable unstructured text; parsing markdown tables or markdown‑formatted code blocks inside a React UI requires heavy frontend handling and fragile regex parsers.
  • Modern engineering teams want models embedded inside Cursor Agent, GitHub actions, or terminal scripts using Claude Code, not locked inside yet another browser tab.
  • Managing custom chat UIs across multi‑model setups means updating frontend streaming adapters every time Google drops Gemini 3.1 or Meta pushes Llama 4 updates.

📊 Models & Output Formats

Model Output format
GPT‑5.6 Sol Ultra Structured JSON (strict)
Claude Sonnet 5 Structured JSON (strict)
Claude Mythos 5 Strict binary or JSON
GPT‑5.5 Strict binary or JSON

💡 Why it matters

  • Reducing token traffic lowers costs and latency for simple state changes.
  • Structured JSON responses can be consumed directly as code parameters or database mutations, eliminating fragile UI‑level parsing.
  • Removing the frontend UI eliminates the need to maintain streaming adapters and markdown parsers whenever underlying models are upgraded.

🚀 Future direction

  • The architectural shift away from chat UIs relies heavily on three core technologies: standardized protocol schemas like MCP, structured tool calling natively backed by models, and event‑driven background queues.
  • In the modern headless pipeline, software systems communicate directly with agent microservices, with context and state handled by external memory frameworks and vector stores.

item.title: Agentic AI Design Patterns and Visual Workflow Builders Gain Traction in 2026
item.description:
Agentic AI Design Patterns and Visual Workflow Builders Gain Traction in 2026

🔍 Overview

Agentic AI design patterns—reusable blueprints that tell an AI agent how to reason, act, and improve its own work—are becoming the core of production‑grade AI agents. 2026 sees these patterns packaged in frameworks like LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI, while visual workflow builders such as Workflow Builder, Dify, Langflow, n8n, and Sim make the engineering of complex agentic systems easier.

🧩 Core Agentic AI Design Patterns

  • Reflection – the agent drafts output, critiques it against clear criteria, then revises. It adds virtually no cost because it requires no new tools, only an extra pass. Research (Reflexion, Self‑Refine) shows that a weaker model wrapped in a reflection loop can beat a stronger model used zero‑shot.
  • Tool Use – the agent calls APIs, databases, or code to take action (e.g., running tests, reading failures, rewriting code).
  • Planning – the agent breaks a big goal into ordered steps and adapts when a step fails. Two common styles:
    • ReAct interleaves reasoning and action, choosing the next step after each result.
    • Plan‑and‑execute writes the full plan first, runs it, and replans only on failure.
  • Multi‑Agent Collaboration – specialised agents (researcher, coder, reviewer) split work and hand results to each other. Centralised coordination improved results by roughly 81 % on parallelisable tasks in Google Research tests, while poorly designed multi‑agent variants degraded performance by 39‑70 %.

⚙️ Implementations & Frameworks

  • LangGraph, Microsoft AutoGen, CrewAI – ship the four patterns as building blocks. Andrew Ng popularised the framing in 2024, and the same patterns appear in Anthropic’s guide to effective agents.
  • Production advice – combine two or three patterns: a core reasoning or planning loop, tools for action, and reflection for quality. Add multi‑agent setups only when sub‑tasks are genuinely independent. Cap retries at two or three and prefer external signals (unit tests, linters, schema validators) over self‑opinion.
  • Cost and risk – Gartner expects over 40 % of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 due to rising costs, unclear value, and weak risk controls. The simplest pattern that solves the task is usually the right one.

📊 Choosing Visual Workflow Builders

Builder Primary Strength Ideal Use Case
Workflow Builder Embedded visual editor that lives inside a product Customer‑facing AI products needing an in‑app authoring layer
Dify All‑in‑one platform for building, testing, and deploying AI applications Internal AI products, prototyping, teams wanting a single system for the lifecycle
Langflow Rapid composition of agentic and RAG flows with strong Python ecosystem Python‑based agents and Retrieval‑Augmented Generation workflows

Sim Modern open‑source workspace with visual workflows, deployment, versioning Teams wanting open‑source flexibility and version control
Flowise (Archived) End of life announced August 2026; no longer a live option

Selection tips – Consider who will author the workflows, which system will handle execution, and how much control you need over the user experience and workflow data.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Gartner forecasts that 33 % of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI by 2028, up from under 1 % in 2024.
  • In production, a sound agent architecture (core reasoning/planning + tools + reflection) matters more than the underlying LLM model.
  • Visual workflow builders reduce the engineering burden by letting teams define, inspect, and change agent behavior without turning every adjustment into code.
  • Properly scoped patterns—using reflection for quality, planning for multi‑step tasks, and restrained multi‑agent collaboration—help keep token usage, latency, and cost under control while delivering reliable, testable AI agents.

item.title: AI Engineering Loop Becomes Mainstream with Agentic Tools and Structured Workflow
item.description:
AI Engineering Loop Becomes Mainstream with Agentic Tools and Structured Workflow

In 2025‑2026 a set of agentic tools and a disciplined engineering loop displaced the myth of one‑shot prompting for software development.

🔍 Overview

  • Most disappointed AI projects assume software can be built with a single prompt – the “one‑shot prompting” myth.
  • AI engineering is actually iterative, incremental, and planning‑heavy.
  • The industry split: some think AI writes the software, others see AI as a candidate generator that needs a disciplined loop to become production code.

🗓️ Timeline of Key Milestones

  • 2020 – Retrieval‑augmented generation introduced.
  • 2022‑2023 – Tool‑use and reasoning loops (the ReAct pattern) landed.
  • 2023‑2024 – Agents and the “harness” idea followed.
  • Late 2024 – Model Context Protocol published.
  • 2025 – Claude Code moved from preview to general availability.
  • April 2025 – GitHub Copilot agent mode rolled out to stable.
  • October 2025 – Agent Skills and the SKILL.md convention arrived; through 2026 the pattern went mainstream with a skills marketplace, industry plugins, cloud‑hosted managed agents, and multi‑agent workflows.
  • Late 2025 onward – Models follow written guidelines and guardrails reliably, making a governed, file‑based agentic setup production‑viable.

♻️ The AI Engineering Loop

  1. Plan deeply – Write the destination as behavior (≈ 500 words). Include Out of Scope and Assumptions.
  2. Generate fast – The agent builds vertical slices, starting with the riskiest unknown (a tracer bullet through the whole stack).
  3. Verify hard – Read the code; judgment is checked here. Passing tests is not “done”; it unlocks the next loop.
  4. Own the result – Findings become new issues that feed back into generation.
  5. Repeat – Each pass ships a thin, verified slice; the loop is tight, not skipped.

📊 Evidence of Impact

  • The 70 % problem (Addy Osmani): AI reliably nails the first ~70 % of a task – scaffolding, boilerplate, common patterns.
  • The remaining 30 % requires human judgment.
  • Code can be produced at roughly 1,600 lines a day but safely reviewed at about 400 lines an hour – four hours of careful review for every day of output.
  • 84 % of developers now use or plan to use AI tools, yet only about a third trust the output.
  • One‑shot prompting is the fastest way to “rack it up”, but the fix is cultural: replace dump‑and‑review with verify‑then‑merge.

🚀 Tool Availability

  • Claude Code – General availability in 2025.
  • GitHub Copilot agent mode – Stable release in April 2025.
  • Agent Skills & SKILL.md – Introduced Oct 2025; now mainstream through 2026 with a skills marketplace and multi‑agent workflows.
  • Models from late 2025 onward reliably follow written guardrails, enabling production‑grade, file‑based agentic setups.

The shift from a single prompt to a repeatable, verified loop delivers faster generation while preserving safety and quality.

item.title: NVIDIA cuPhoton GPU Toolkit Accelerates End-to-End Astronomical Image Processing
item.description:
NVIDIA cuPhoton GPU Toolkit Accelerates End-to-End Astronomical Image Processing

NVIDIA released cuPhoton 0.1.3, an open‑source CUDA‑X toolkit that moves the entire image‑processing path for astronomy, laser, and X‑ray data onto the GPU, collapsing wait times from seconds to minutes and enabling interactive analysis.

🔍 Overview

  • Modern observatories and high‑throughput instruments generate image data faster than CPU‑bound pipelines can process it.
  • The bottleneck spans the whole path: sensor readout, point‑spread‑function (PSF) matching, subtraction, fitting, classification, and alert generation.
  • A GPU‑native path that stays on the GPU from sensor to decision is missing – cuPhoton provides exactly that.

🧩 How it Works

  • cuPhoton implements each stage of the pipeline as GPU‑accelerated building blocks, keeping data resident on the GPU.
  • Typical workflow steps include:
    1. xDataReader – Loads raw sensor data directly into GPU memory.
    2. xRep – Handles PSF‑matching and image subtraction.
    3. xPois – Performs statistical processing of photon events.
    4. xFit – Fits dual‑PSF models to dipoles produced by moving objects.
    5. xScan – Classifies detections as transients or artifacts.
    6. xRay – Specialized for time‑domain X‑ray detector analysis.
Component Role
xDataReader GPU‑resident image loading
xRep PSF‑match and subtraction
xPois Photon‑event processing
xFit Dual‑PSF fitting
xScan Classification of detections
xRay X‑ray time‑domain analysis

⚙️ Key Details

  • Performance: On workloads of hundreds of terabytes, cuPhoton achieved up to 14,900× speedup for image loading and up to 14,550× for signal processing, turning months of CPU time into minutes.
  • End‑to‑end impact: Data analytics that previously required nine months completed in four hours on GPU‑accelerated Python.
  • Latency: For kilobyte‑scale datasets, the entire pipeline runs in milliseconds or microseconds.
  • Scaling: Works on multi‑GPU, multi‑node systems such as NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and NVIDIA Vera Rubin.
  • Supported environments: cuPhoton 0.1.3 runs on Linux with Python 3.12–3.14 and CUDA 13. Building from source needs a C++17 compiler, CUDA and cuFile headers, and a re‑entrant CFITSIO installation.

🚀 Availability 

1

The toolkit is open‑source and part of the NVIDIA CUDA‑X ecosystem.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Instruments like the NSF‑DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory capture a 3.2‑gigapixel exposure every 39 seconds, producing up to 20 TB of images and 10 million candidate objects per night.

item.title: 2025 Marks Shift to Autonomous Multi‑Agent AI Systems
item.description:
2025 Marks Shift to Autonomous Multi‑Agent AI Systems

In 2025 the AI landscape moved from passive prompt‑response models to autonomous agents that can plan, code, and validate work without constant human direction.

🔍 Overview

  • Earlier language models waited for explicit human instruction at every computational step.
  • Modern autonomous AI trends establish continuous‑operation paradigms where systems evaluate high‑level objectives, generate internal sub‑goals, and execute complex workflows without constant human oversight.
  • The human role changes from typist to director.

🧩 How it works

  • Agent architecture maintains state and uses scratchpads for intermediate reasoning, looping until validation criteria pass.
  • Probabilistic reasoning engines evaluate environment states, select optimal tools, and modify execution paths dynamically.
  • When data is missing or errors occur, the system queries internal memory, tests alternative APIs, or restructures the execution tree autonomously.
  • Multi‑agent collaboration divides massive operational workloads into manageable micro‑tasks.
Agent Type Role
Planner Evaluates high‑level objectives and creates internal sub‑goals
Coder Generates code to implement the sub‑goals
QA Reviewer Validates output against criteria and provides feedback
  • Frameworks such as LangGraph and AutoGen orchestrate communication protocols between instances.

⚙️ Key details

  • Traditional software runs deterministic branching logic; autonomous systems use probabilistic reasoning and dynamic tool selection.
  • Heavy models run in centralized cloud data centers incur high latency and compute cost.
  • Hardware manufacturers now ship specialized NPUs to consumer and enterprise edge devices, enabling local inference, cutting round‑trip time, and keeping proprietary data off third‑party servers.
  • Autonomous deployment agents monitor CI/CD pipelines, detect performance regressions, isolate faulty micro‑services, patch Kubernetes configurations, and execute zero‑downtime rollouts. Human engineers intervene only for high‑risk architectural changes or policy approvals.
  • Autonomous agents can ingest real‑time shipping telemetry, customs databases, and weather feeds to recalculate optimal routes, renegotiate carrier contracts, and reroute cargo instantly.
  • In finance, agents execute portfolio‑hedging strategies instantly, bypassing human reaction latency during flash crashes or sudden market shifts.

🔒 Security considerations

  • CRITICAL SECURITY WARNING: Autonomous agents with write permissions to production databases or cloud infrastructure are a severe vector for catastrophic failure.
  • Always implement deterministic validation gates and human‑in‑the‑loop checkpoints before executing irreversible write operations, database migrations, or financial transactions that exceed defined thresholds.
  • Restrict agent permissions to scoped, ephemeral tokens with minimal necessary privileges.

💡 Why it matters

  • Shifts AI from reactive text generation to proactive task execution, closing the feedback loop between failure and remediation.
  • Reduces latency, compute cost, and reliance on centralized cloud resources.
  • Enables real‑time adaptation to volatile global trade conditions and fast‑moving financial markets.

On 5 October 2026 Anthropic announced a new version of its Cowork product that moves both model inference and the supporting virtual machine (VM) from the local device to the cloud.

🔍 Overview

  • The old version of Cowork runs model inference in the cloud but executes tool calls in an Anthropic‑provided VM shipped to the user’s computer.

  • Users also disliked that closing a laptop caused work to stop.

🧩 How it Works

  • Each session receives its own sandbox in the cloud; state is not shared with other sessions.
  • When the cloud‑based VM needs a local resource (e.g., a file), the desktop app performs the required file‑access tool call.
  • This architecture lets Cowork run on phones, keep work running when a laptop is closed, and deliver the same compute power without draining the device’s battery.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Inference location: Cloud (both old and new versions).
  • VM location: Local (old) → Cloud (new).
  • Session isolation: Per‑session sandbox, no cross‑session state sharing.
  • Local file access: Handled by the desktop application via tool calls.
  • User‑reported pain points addressed: Disk usage, battery drain, performance overhead, and interruption when the laptop is closed.
  • Quote: “We think this solves a lot of problems we’ve heard about (like using Cowork from a phone, keeping work running, or getting all the same power without losing battery to the VM)” — Felix Rieseberg, Anthropic, see also this help page.

item.title: Graphectory Enables Process‑Centric Analysis and Real‑Time Monitoring of Agentic Systems
item.description:
Graphectory Enables Process‑Centric Analysis and Real‑Time Monitoring of Agentic Systems

Agentic systems are modern software systems composed of orchestrated modules, exposed interfaces, and deployment pipelines. Their execution is stochastic and adaptive, and evaluation has traditionally been outcome‑centric, focusing only on final success or failure. To expose how agents reason, plan, act, and adjust strategies, researchers introduced Graphectory, a systematic encoding of temporal and semantic relations in such software.

🔍 Overview

  • Agentic workflows such as SWE‑agent and OpenHands were examined.
  • Analyses covered 4,000 trajectories generated with a combination of four backbone Large Language Models (LLMs).
  • The goal was to resolve issues from the SWE‑bench Verified benchmark.

🧩 How Graphectory Works

  • Inspired by graph representations of conventional software, Graphectory records the sequence of actions, decisions, and context changes as a directed graph.
  • This representation supports the creation of process‑centric metrics that assess workflow quality beyond final outcomes.
  • An accompanying technique, Langutory, captures language‑level information alongside the graph.

📊 Findings from Automated Analyses

  • The full analysis completed in four minutes.
  • Richer prompts or stronger LLMs produced more complex Graphectory graphs, indicating deeper exploration, broader context gathering, and more thorough validation before submitting patches.
  • Problem‑solving strategies depended on problem difficulty and the underlying LLM:
    • For resolved issues, agents typically followed a coherent localization → patching → validation pattern.
    • Unresolved issues often displayed chaotic, repetitive, or back‑tracking behaviors.
  • Even when successful, agents frequently followed inefficient processes, leading to unnecessarily long trajectories.

⚙️ Real‑Time Construction and Intervention

  • A novel technique builds Graphectory and Langutory in real time during execution.
  • When the system detects trajectory issues, it sends a diagnostic message to the agent and can roll back the trajectory when appropriate.
  • Experimental results show that online monitoring with interventions improves resolution rates by 6.9%–23.5% across models for problematic instances, while significantly shortening trajectories with near‑zero overhead.

🚀 Why It Matters

  • Shifts evaluation from a purely outcome‑centric view to a process‑centric perspective, enabling deeper insight into agent reasoning.
  • Provides a practical pathway to enhance agentic programming productivity through automated, low‑overhead monitoring and corrective feedback.
  • Establishes a foundation for future research on systematic, graph‑based analysis of stochastic AI workflows.

Phase Function

Build Engineering constructs the feature
Test QA checks the work
Release A release system takes over deployment
Learn Analytics provides feedback on what happened afterward

⚙️ Key details

Research indicates significant gaps in how product information is currently documented and handled by both humans and AI agents.

Capturing institutional memory is critical because simple technical changes do not require much memory, but complex product logic often does. item.title: Dogwood Local Engine released as Apache‑2.0 library for temporal policy enforcement
item.description:
Dogwood Local Engine released as Apache‑2.0 library for temporal policy enforcement

Today we are releasing the Dogwood Local Engine under the Apache 2.0 license. The engine embeds the Dogwood governance language to enforce agent actions with temporal conditions.

🔍 Overview

  • Dogwood is an open source governance language for agents and their actions, released in August.
  • Policies specify which actions an agent may take and under what conditions, including temporal conditions that refer to past actions and outcomes.

🧩 How it works

  • The engine can be embedded as a library into an enforcement layer that regulates agents’ tool calls.
  • It maintains a durable record of past actions, tracking the order, timing, and outcomes so it can survive crashes and restart.
  • Only request events receive allow/deny verdicts; response events record outcomes (e.g., test pass/fail) used by temporal clauses.
  • An event is a timestamped record of one step of a tool call. A tool call typically generates a request event and a response event, forming the history evaluated by the engine.

⚙️ Key details

  • Supports dynamic policy updates without pausing workflows.
  • Example policies:
    • run_tests: the agent may always run the tests.
    • push_after_green_tests: the agent may push only when a test run has passed within the last fifteen minutes and no run has failed since. The when temporal clause expresses this condition.
  • The temporal clause is evaluated against the event history; it depends on events that happened before the request.

🚀 Availability

  • Released under the Apache 2.0 open source license.
  • Available as a local engine library that can be embedded.

💡 Why it matters

  • Allows policies to depend on past actions, their outcomes, order, and timing.
  • Guarantees enforcement after crashes because the engine stores history durably.
  • Supports policy changes during a session without stopping the workflow.

New Frameworks for Governing AI Coding Agent Costs and Research Diversity

Recent developments in AI agent deployment address the challenges of enterprise cost management for coding agents and the optimization of multi-agent systems for alpha factor mining.

⚙️ Coding Agent Governance

Enterprises are scaling AI coding agents from small pilots to tens of thousands of seats, often utilizing “harnesses” from vendors such as OpenAI’s Codex or Anthropic’s Claude Code. These harnesses control model selection, prompt cache usage, and subagent execution, which determines the final cost.

To manage these expenses, a new customizable router has been developed featuring:

  • Jev: A classifier using calibrated probabilities to label prompts against a custom taxonomy of agentic requests.
  • Strategic Routing: Work is moved only at session start, in side lanes, and at subagent launch to avoid rebuilding prompt caches.
  • Cost Analysis: Data from 10,000 real sessions shows that on long, tool-heavy sessions, the highest-priced model can cost less than the next tier.

In an emulated enterprise of 10,000 seats, this router recovered between 14% and 21% of model spend based on Anthropic’s September 21, 2026, list prices, totaling $3.3M to $5.0M annually.

🧩 AlphaDiverse Framework

To address limitations in control, availability, and confidentiality associated with external APIs in alpha factor mining, the AlphaDiverse framework has been proposed. It integrates a multi-agent research system with post-training for local agents.

Key technical components include:

  • Diverse Path Collection: The system generates complementary plan portfolios and varies research environments across loops to prevent research path collapse.
  • Local Agent Tuning: Supervised fine-tuning is used to warm-start local Planner and Realizer agents using diverse traces.
  • Joint GRPO Method: An optimization method used to improve both agents based on the diversity of contributions and predictive quality.
  • Evaluation: To avoid test-set tuning, research feedback is limited to inner period data, while a frozen final model is evaluated on outer period data.

Experiments across four Chinese stock universes indicate that AlphaDiverse combines broader exploration with competitive prediction.

New Method Reduces Tool-Call Costs for Updating Tool-Using AI Agents

Researchers have developed a method to maintain action credit for tool-using agents after policy updates, reducing the need to recompute data from scratch through the reuse and correction of historical evidence.

🧩 How it works

The approach introduces several mechanisms to manage how agents handle action credit after a policy update:

  • Pairwise branch sensitivity: Captures how strongly a policy update affects downstream regions that distinguish two candidate actions.
  • First-order anchored credit-transport estimator: Updates historical credit using old interventional trajectories.
  • Decision-Sufficient Credit Gate (DSC-Gate): A system that chooses whether to reuse, transport, or resample credit.

⚙️ Key details

Experiments indicated that branch sensitivity is a more substantial explanation for credit drift than global policy distance. When sufficient historical data is available, credit transport reduces estimation error, specifically on updates affecting action-distinguishing branches.

💡 Why it matters

Recomputing action credits from scratch after every policy update can be expensive, requiring many additional tool calls and environment interactions. This new approach demonstrates that agents do not need to recompute credit every time.

On a fully independent test set, the DSC-Gate showed the following results relative to a gap-based gate:

Metric Result
Mean Regret Change +0.00004
Mean New Tool Steps Reduced from 472 to 286 (39.4% reduction)

These patterns were also observed after a real tool-agent parameter update.

Introduction of JAZ Framework for Minimalist LLM Agent Development

Researchers have developed JAZ, an LLM agent framework designed to investigate the effectiveness of a minimal harness consisting primarily of an agent loop. By focusing on simplicity, the framework aims to perform tasks usually handled by specialized systems.

🧩 How it works

item.title: Introduction of Hill Sampling for Program Edit Optimization in LLMs
item.description:
Introduction of Hill Sampling for Program Edit Optimization in LLMs

Researchers have introduced Hill Sampling, a procedure designed to improve program edits by repeatedly sampling from a frozen Large Language Model (LLM).

🧩 How it works

Hill Sampling follows a specific iterative process:

  • It repeatedly samples candidate program edits from a frozen LLM.
  • It retains the best program found during the process.
  • All subsequent samples are conditioned on that best program.

⚙️ Key details

The method was evaluated using three open-weight models across the following problems:

Problem Result
Circle packing Sets a new state of the art among published methods
Erdos’ minimum-overlap problem Improves over the AlphaEvolve reference
Sums and differences of finite sets Achieves strong results

Performance on circle packing and Erdos results required hours of wall-clock time using eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

💡 Why it matters

The researchers also conducted a study on evolution strategies (ES) applied to LLM weights at test time, finding that:

  • Learning the weights performed worse than setting the ES learning rate to zero.
  • While fixed random perturbations in weight space can help exploration, randomness from token sampling is stronger.
  • Repeated sampling remains substantially weaker than Hill Sampling.

These findings suggest a test-time compute allocation strategy: repeatedly sample edits to the best verified solution found so far before implementing more complex mechanisms like diversity mechanisms, evolutionary scaffolds, archives, or test-time parameter learning.

#LLM #HillSampling #ProgramSynthesis #EvolutionStrategies

Source: Hill Sampling for Test-Time Scaling: A Simple and Better Alternative to Repeated Sampling, Evolution, and Training

item.title: SWE-Serve Benchmark Evaluates AI Agents on Inference-Serving Stack Changes
item.description:
SWE-Serve Benchmark Evaluates AI Agents on Inference-Serving Stack Changes

Researchers have introduced SWE-Serve, a benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of AI agents to handle repository-scale changes across the inference-serving stack.

🔍 Overview

SWE-Serve evaluates gaps in AI agent performance by testing changes to SGLang, an open-source system for serving large language models. The benchmark turns 83 merged SGLang pull requests into 53 executable tasks across six inference-engineering families, including:

  • Model enablement
  • Decoding
  • Caching
  • Scheduling
  • Serving APIs
  • Runtime performance

⚙️ Key Details

Tasks in the benchmark are distributed by hardware and scope:

  • Hardware: 12 tasks run on CPU and 41 use a single NVIDIA H100.
  • Task Composition: 37 tasks originate from a single upstream pull request, while 16 combine two to six related changes.
  • Complexity: The median reference solution involves modifying 553 lines across seven files.
  • Verification: A typical verifier includes seven tests for new behavior and 10 regression tests. A patch passes if it satisfies a hidden verifier on the declared hardware.

🧩 How it works

SWE-Serve includes 19 tasks that utilize a live serving interface to test patches. These 19 tasks contain 276 live serving tests, 242 of which are sourced or adapted from SGLang. Additionally, three tasks enforce a calibrated performance gate on an H100.

One specific task requires an agent to add serving support for Qwen3.5 models; the agent must ensure both the 0.8B dense model and the 35B-A3B MoE model load and serve through normal SGLang interfaces on one H100.

💡 Why it matters

Evaluation using mini-swe-agent—a minimal software-engineering agent using only Bash under closed-book conditions—revealed a performance gap when live-serving checks are applied:

  • Live Serving Impact: Across 19 tasks, patches passed 69.4% of the time when live-serving checks were excluded, but only 45.9% with the complete verifier.
  • Failure Rate: Approximately one in three patches that passed other checks failed live-serving tests. Specifically, 16 of 33 patches passed every other check but failed at least one live serving test.
  • Domain Complexity: Tasks confined to one runtime domain had a 69.0% pass rate, whereas tasks spanning more than one runtime domain had a 47.7% pass rate.

Across 11 models and 31 model-effort configurations, mean pass@1 ranged from 34.6% to 75.5%. Agent sessions were capped at 350 steps and 210 minutes.

item.title: Introduction of tokenizers v1 with SIMD and Parallelism Improvements
item.description:
Introduction of tokenizers v1 with SIMD and Parallelism Improvements

A new version of the tokenizers library, v1, has been released. The goal of this version was to improve performance while preserving the API, vocabulary, merge ranks, and output of v0.23, ensuring v1 produces the same token IDs as the previous version.

🧩 How it works

Tokenizers run conversions in four stages:

Stage Description
Normalization Applies operations such as Unicode normalization or lowercasing to raw text.
Pre-tokenization Splits text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens.
Model Maps each pre-token to IDs in its vocabulary.
Post-processing Adds special tokens expected by the model.

⚙️ Key details

BPE and Model Support

  • The library supports three model types: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE), WordPiece, and Unigram.
  • Eight of the ten measured model families use BPE.
  • BPE models use regular expressions to split input text into pre-tokens; merges occur inside a pre-token and never across boundaries.

Performance Optimizations

  • SIMD Instructions: For a handful of common grammars, a hand-written function uses SIMD instructions to find splits via boolean operations over bitstreams instead of a regex engine. This process, using bitcannon, views input bytes as parallel streams and decides 64 bytes per register operation.
  • Memory Management: The merge working set uses a caller-owned scratch buffer to avoid touching the allocator. Merged pieces form an intrusive doubly-linked list inside one preallocated buffer, allowing merges to update two indices rather than moving data.
  • Caching: A thread-local memo maps pre-token bytes to finished IDs, allowing repeated words to be merged once.
  • Concurrency: Each thread draws its scratch buffer and word cache from its own sub-pool, allowing one shared tokenizer to encode from many threads at once without queuing on a single lock.

Architecture Changes

  • The library remains general across tokenizer families and loads everything v0.23 loaded.
  • The project structure moved from one crate to a workspace:
    • tk-encode: The required runtime.
    • tk-serialize, tk-convert, and tk-train: Linked only when an application needs them.

Researchers have introduced LLM-as-an-Improver and a method called Verify–Repair–Reselect (VRR) to enhance the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by using verification feedback to generate and reselect improved candidates.

🧩 How it works

VRR builds upon verifier-based selection, which typically improves performance by generating multiple candidate solutions and using a verifier to select the most promising one. The VRR process operates as follows:

  • Candidate Generation: The system retains the initial winner and conditionally generates three complementary alternatives:
    • A repaired version of the winner.
    • A repaired version of the runner-up.
    • A solution based on a new approach.
  • Filtering: It uses only inference-time information to filter out duplicate and invalid candidates.
  • Reselection: The final answer is reselected based on the original evaluation criteria.

💡 Why it matters

Testing across diverse models and reasoning and code-generation benchmarks shows that VRR:

  • Improves over fixed-pool verifier-based selection in many settings.
  • Can recover correct solutions even in instances where all candidates in the initial pool were incorrect.

item.description:
Consistency Guidelines for ALTK-Evolve Reduce Agent Reliability Gaps

An update to the ALTK-Evolve system introduces consistency guidelines designed to address the reliability gap in AI agents, where workflows that succeed once may fail upon repeated requests.

💡 Why it matters

Reliability is a critical issue for mission-critical work, such as checking a contract for an obligation or reconciling a financial transaction. This inconsistency is not a capability problem solvable by larger models, but an orthogonal axis where an agent can be simultaneously capable and inconsistent.

🔍 Overview

Using a ReAct agent (GPT-4.1 on AppWorld test_normal), researchers identified a “consistency gap”—defined as Mean@k minus Pass^k. While the agent posted a Mean@5 of 77.4%, its Pass^5 was only 53.0%, resulting in a 24.4-point consistency gap. On hard tasks, this gap reaches 30 points.

This variance occurs because LLM decisions are based on probability distributions over next tokens:

  • Sharp distributions: Most mass is on a single token, making them resilient to platform-side effects like request batching or GPU floating-point non-associativity.
  • Flat distributions: Mass is spread across near-tied tokens. Small perturbations on hosted endpoints can reorder these ties, causing the same prompt at temperature 0.0 to resolve differently from run to run.

🧩 How it works

The update introduces consistency guidelines built upon a diagnostic tool called the Consistency Analyzer.

  • Diagnosis: The Consistency Analyzer resamples an agent’s recorded trajectory to find “flip-prone decision points” where the model was one token-sample away from a different action.
  • Process: It requires one trace and no ground truth. It resamples each decision point in the trace with a single call requesting k completions (k=5 by default) replayed against the recorded context, rather than re-running the task end-to-end.
  • Implementation: These diagnoses are turned into guidelines and injected back at inference time.

⚙️ Key details

Turning the Consistency Analyzer’s diagnosis into guidelines resulted in the following improvements:

Metric Impact
Consistency Gap Halved from 24.4pp to 12.0pp
Same-task Pass^5 +16.0pp
Similar-task +13.0pp
Average Accuracy No cost

The setup utilized a ReAct agent running at temperature 0.0.

🔍 Overview

A harness in this context refers to the runtime around an agent, including its tools, memory, guardrails, triggering workflows, dependent services, and the protocols used by other agents to reach it. Go Micro provides this harness as Go code.

🧩 How it works

Go Micro allows for the description of a system, which it then uses to design services, write handlers, compile them, and start them. Key capabilities include:

  • Connectivity: Agents are reachable via MCP and A2A.

  • Orchestration: Durable flows are used to orchestrate deterministic parts of the system.
  • Dynamic Development: If an agent requires a capability that does not exist, it can build the service mid-conversation.
  • Code Management: Generated code is plain Go on disk, which can be edited by hand; re-running the process preserves these changes.

Every generator in the plugin writes a working, deployable piece of an application. Multiplayer Agent Harness for Collaborative Work in Slack and Web

A new multiplayer agent harness for work has been introduced, enabling employees to work independently in isolated workspaces or collaborate with an agent in projects, group messages, and Slack channels.

🔍 Overview

The system allows users to customize their own agent while maintaining the ability to work collaboratively. Identity and configuration are consistent between the web app and Slack. Key capabilities include:

  • Internal Search: Search across the web, databases, documents, email, and internal notes.

  • Project Tracking: Post follow-ups and updates in shared channels to track projects.
  • App Creation: Build and publish custom internal apps to specific people.

🧩 How it works

Each person and room is provided with its own scoped memory, permissions, files, keychain view, durable sandbox, crons, and web apps.

  • Core Architecture: The core runs TypeScript on Node and uses Fastify for HTTP. A Postgres persistence layer manages session history, user data, and other durable state.
  • Integration: The web UI, public portal, and admin panel are optional plugins over the core’s HTTP API. Slack is an optional in-process plugin supervised through a direct service client.
  • Tooling: The agent uses a small, fixed tool surface. The execute tool allows the agent to run commands in its own isolated, durable sandbox where installed tools remain installed.
  • Tech Stack: The Slack plugin uses Bolt, while the web UI utilizes Vite for builds and Lit for rendering.

Strict Every harness tool call requires human approval, except for two no-effect turn enders.
Auto (default) A classifier screens tool results and provenance-labelled external data; deployments can use their own screening proxy.
Dangerous No pauses between tool calls and no content screening.

Regardless of the posture, a predeclared command policy applies to provide hard denials and approval rules for destructive SQL or recursive deletes.
